IAM.concepts: Identity & Access Management authenticates every actor and authorizes every action. There is no unauthenticated path and no unaudited grant. Identity (who you are), Authentication (proof), Authorization (what you may do), and Delegation (on whose behalf) are four separate, governed concerns.
IAM.ontology: IAM binds an Identity to Authentication evidence to an Authority scope to a Permission set. Permissions are granted, never assumed; every grant is reversible and traceable to its granter.
IAM.taxonomy: By actor: Human / Agent / Service / System. By factor: Passwordless / MFA / Hardware-key / Certificate / Token / Biometric. By scope: Platform / Tenant / Context / Instance.
IAM.dataModel:
```yaml
AccessGrant:
  grantId: <Identity>
  subject: <Identity>
  authority: <Authority>
  permissions: [<registry permission>]
  scope: <Context>
  temporal: {grantedAt, expiresAt}
  delegatedFrom: <Grant|null>
  conditions: [<registry expression>]
```
IAM.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested
    Requested --> Authenticated
    Authenticated --> Authorized
    Authorized --> Granted
    Granted --> Active
    Active --> Expired
    Active --> Revoked
    Expired --> [*]
    Revoked --> [*]
```
workflow: authenticate with registered factors → resolve authority scope → evaluate permissions under context → grant with expiry → revoke on demand or expiry
authorities: IAM Authority issues grants; granter's authority bounds the grant — rights are monotone-decreasing down the delegation chain.
IAM.privacy: Authentication evidence is never stored in plaintext; biometrics never leave the device enclave. Grants reference scopes, not personal contents.
IAM.audit: Every authentication and authorization is logged with factor strength, grant chain, and decision rationale.
IAM.twin: IAM twin monitors grant sprawl, stale grants, and authentication failure patterns as security signals.
IAM.agent: Security agent detects anomalous grant patterns and over-broad delegations, revoking or escalating under policy.
IAM.runtime: Authorization is evaluated per request, cached per (subject, permission, policy-version) with event-driven invalidation on revoke.
IAM.scaling: Auth is the hottest security path — token verification is stateless; grant resolution is cached and short-TTL.
IAM.multiTenant: Grants are tenant-scoped; cross-tenant grants require both tenants' authorities and are heavily audited.
IAM.geo: Authentication evidence and grant logs reside in-jurisdiction; cross-region auth respects residency.
IAM.failure: Grant cycle, rights inflation, stale grant after revocation storm, factor unavailability.
IAM.recovery: Grants are event-sourced; revocation cascades to all derived grants immediately.
IAM.certification: Every grant must be traceable to constitutional authority — untraceable grants are denied by default.
IAM.migration: New factors and permission types are registry additions.
IAM.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Actor
    participant IA as IAM
    participant AU as Authority
    A->>IA: authenticate(factors)
    IA-->>A: identity
    A->>IA: authorize(action, context)
    IA->>AU: resolve grant chain
    AU-->>IA: scope
    IA-->>A: decision
```
IAM.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Verifying
    Verifying --> Resolving
    Resolving --> Evaluating
    Evaluating --> Deciding
```
IAM.blueprint: Build order for IAM: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by actor: human / agent / service / system as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (iam.authenticate, iam.authorize, iam.grant) and validate against IAM boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

ZTA.concepts: Zero Trust Architecture assumes no implicit trust anywhere. Every request is authenticated, authorized, encrypted, and evidenced — regardless of network location. 'Inside the network' is not a concept the platform recognizes.
ZTA.ontology: Zero Trust is a property of every interaction: Identity verified, Context evaluated, Policy enforced, Least-privilege applied, Session bounded, and Everything logged. Trust is computed per request, never cached across sessions.
ZTA.taxonomy: By enforcement: Per-request / Per-session / Per-flow. By network: Mesh / Perimeter-less / Segmented. By evidence: Cryptographic / Behavioral / Attestation-based.
ZTA.dataModel:
```yaml
ZeroTrustDecision:
  decisionId: <Identity>
  subject: <Identity>
  resource: <registry resource>
  context: <Context>
  trustScore: <Trust>
  policyVersion: <version>
  decision: <Allow|Deny|StepUp|Challenge>
  evidence: [<Evidence>]
  temporal: {at}
```
ZTA.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Evaluating
    Evaluating --> Allowed
    Evaluating --> Denied
    Evaluating --> StepUp: trust marginal
    StepUp --> Allowed: factor satisfied
    StepUp --> Denied
    Allowed --> Quarantined: post-allow anomaly
```
workflow: identify → score trust in context → evaluate least-privilege policy → allow / step-up / deny → continuously verify post-allow
authorities: Zero Trust Authority (policy); decisions are per-request and never delegated implicitly.
ZTA.privacy: Behavioral evidence is minimized and consent-scoped; post-allow monitoring targets patterns, not contents.
ZTA.audit: Every decision — allow and deny — is logged with trust inputs, policy version, and evidence. Denials are first-class audit artifacts.
ZTA.twin: Zero Trust twin monitors decision latency, denial rates, and step-up friction as security UX signals.
ZTA.agent: Zero Trust agent continuously re-evaluates active sessions and revokes on trust decay.
ZTA.runtime: Evaluation is in-line on every request; mTLS is mandatory service-to-service; no plaintext internal traffic exists.
ZTA.scaling: Evaluation is cached per (subject, resource, policy-version) with short TTL; trust decay invalidates.
ZTA.multiTenant: Tenant isolation is enforced at every layer — network, compute, storage — never assumed from segmentation.
ZTA.geo: Attestation and decision logs reside in-jurisdiction; cross-region requests are re-evaluated, not trusted.
ZTA.failure: Trust staleness, policy version skew, attestation failure, evaluation timeout (default deny).
ZTA.recovery: Quarantine is the safe state; recovery is governed re-attestation, never automatic.
ZTA.certification: Platform must prove no implicit-trust path exists — every flow carries a decision record.
ZTA.migration: New trust factors are registry additions.
ZTA.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Actor
    participant ZT as Zero Trust
    participant TR as Trust
    A->>ZT: request(resource)
    ZT->>TR: compute per-request trust
    TR-->>ZT: score
    ZT->>ZT: least-privilege policy
    alt allow
        ZT-->>A: allowed
    else marginal
        ZT-->>A: step-up required
    end
```
ZTA.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Identifying
    Identifying --> TrustScoring
    TrustScoring --> PolicyEvaluating
    PolicyEvaluating --> Deciding
```
ZTA.blueprint: Build order for ZTA: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by enforcement: per-request / per-session / per-flow as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (zt.evaluate, zt.stepUp, zt.attest) and validate against ZTA boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

CRY.concepts: Cryptography Architecture provides the mathematical foundations: confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation. Cryptographic agility is constitutional — algorithms are registry entries, not constants, so the platform re-keys and re-algorithms without redesign.
CRY.ontology: Cryptography has Algorithm suites (registry), Key references (never raw keys), Operations (sign/verify/encrypt/decrypt/hash/kdf/mac), and Agility policy (rotation schedule, sunset triggers).
CRY.taxonomy: By purpose: Signing / Encryption / Hashing / KDF / MAC / Key-agreement / Zero-knowledge. By agility: Fixed-schedule / Event-triggered / Quantum-ready. By scope: Platform / Tenant / Context.
CRY.dataModel:
```yaml
CryptoOperation:
  opId: <Identity>
  operation: <registry id>
  algorithmSuite: <registry id, versioned>
  keyRef: <KMS reference, never raw>
  inputRef: <content-addressed>
  outputRef: <content-addressed>
  temporal: {at}
  evidence: <Evidence>
```
CRY.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested
    Requested --> SuiteResolved
    SuiteResolved --> KeyResolved
    KeyResolved --> Executed
    Executed --> Evidenced
    Evidenced --> [*]
```
workflow: resolve suite from registry → resolve key reference → execute → record evidence → never expose raw key material
authorities: Cryptography Authority (suite governance); keys are held by KMS and referenced, never handled.
CRY.privacy: Encryption is the baseline for personal data at rest and in transit; plaintext personal data must never exist outside an enclave.
CRY.audit: Every operation records suite version, key reference, and result — without ever recording key material.
CRY.twin: Cryptography twin monitors algorithm usage distribution and sunset exposure across the fleet.
CRY.agent: Cryptography agent detects weak-suite usage and tracks sunset deadlines, driving rotation under governance.
CRY.runtime: Operations are stateless and content-addressed; raw keys never enter process memory outside the KMS boundary.
CRY.scaling: Signing/verification are the hot path — batched and hardware-accelerated where available.
CRY.multiTenant: Keys are tenant-isolated in KMS; cryptographic separation is a boundary, not an assumption.
CRY.geo: Key residency follows data residency; cross-region crypto respects sovereignty (e.g., sovereign-key requirements).
CRY.failure: Suite deprecation, key compromise, verification failure storm, agility gap.
CRY.recovery: Compromise triggers governed rotation + re-signing of affected content-addressed artifacts.
CRY.certification: Every suite in use must be registry-approved and not sunset; raw-key exposure is a critical certification failure.
CRY.migration: Agility is the point — new suites are registry additions, and rotation is a scheduled, not emergency, act.
CRY.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant CR as Crypto
    participant KM as KMS
    C->>CR: sign(payload)
    CR->>CR: resolve suite
    CR->>KM: key reference
    KM-->>CR: operated
    CR->>CR: evidence
    CR-->>C: signature
```
CRY.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SuiteResolving
    SuiteResolving --> KeyResolving
    KeyResolving --> Operating
    Operating --> Evidencing
```

KMS.concepts: Key Management Architecture holds the platform's most sensitive primitive — the keys that make evidence trustworthy. Raw keys never leave KMS; everything else holds references. Key lifecycle is governed, audited, and recoverable only under quorum.
KMS.ontology: Key has an Identity, an Algorithm suite, a Policy (usage, rotation, sunset), a State, and a Custody model. Keys are generated in KMS, referenced everywhere, rotated by policy, destroyed by quorum.
KMS.taxonomy: By custody: Platform / Tenant / Sovereign / Customer-held / HSM-backed. By lifetime: Ephemeral / Short-lived / Long-lived / Eternal. By usage: Signing / Encryption / Wrapping / Derived.
KMS.dataModel:
```yaml
Key:
  keyId: <Identity>
  algorithmSuite: <registry id>
  custody: <registry id>
  usagePolicy: <Policy>
  rotationPolicy: <Policy>
  state: <Active|Rotating|Suspended|Destroyed>
  temporal: {createdAt, rotatesAt, sunsetsAt}
  quorum: {destroyRequires: <n>}
```
KMS.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Generated
    Generated --> Active
    Active --> Rotating: policy schedule
    Rotating --> Active
    Active --> Suspended: suspicion
    Suspended --> Active: cleared
    Suspended --> Destroyed: quorum
    Active --> Destroyed: quorum
    Destroyed --> [*]
```
workflow: generate under policy → reference-only usage → rotate per schedule → suspend on suspicion → destroy only under quorum
authorities: Key Authority (lifecycle); destruction requires quorum — no single principal can destroy a key.
KMS.privacy: Key material is the crown jewel — HSM-backed where available, never logged, never cached outside the boundary.
KMS.audit: Every key operation (including denied ones) is logged; the audit log itself is signed by a separate key.
KMS.twin: KMS twin monitors rotation overdue and key-usage anomalies as critical security signals.
KMS.agent: KMS agent tracks rotation deadlines and flags overdue keys as critical governance failures.
KMS.runtime: All crypto happens inside KMS; callers receive results and references, never material.
KMS.scaling: KMS is the trust bottleneck — horizontally scaled with HSM-backed quorum for critical operations.
KMS.multiTenant: Keys are tenant-isolated by custody; cross-tenant key use is impossible by construction.
KMS.geo: Sovereign keys stay in-jurisdiction; export is prohibited where sovereignty policy forbids.
KMS.failure: Rotation overdue, quorum deadlock, HSM unavailability, key reference leak.
KMS.recovery: Suspended keys can be cleared by quorum; destroyed keys are unrecoverable by design — that irreversibility is the guarantee.
KMS.certification: KMS must prove no raw-key egress path exists — formally audited boundary.
KMS.migration: New custody models are registry additions.
KMS.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Authority
    participant KM as KMS
    participant Q as Quorum
    A->>KM: rotate(key)
    KM->>KM: policy check
    KM->>Q: confirm if destructive
    Q-->>KM: ok
    KM->>KM: rotate, keep history
    KM-->>A: KeyRotated
```
KMS.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Generating
    Generating --> Activating
    Activating --> Serving
    Serving --> Rotating
```
KMS.blueprint: Build order for KMS: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by custody: platform / tenant / sovereign / customer-held / hsm-backed as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (kms.generate, kms.rotate, kms.destroy) and validate against KMS boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

SEC.concepts: Security Runtime Architecture enforces security as an execution-time property, not a review-time aspiration. Every request passes authentication, authorization, policy, trust, and evidence guards — in-line, on the hot path, with no bypass.
SEC.ontology: Security Runtime composes IAM, Zero Trust, Cryptography, KMS, and Policy into a single enforcement pipeline. It is the immune system: detection, prevention, response, and recovery operate continuously.
SEC.taxonomy: By stage: Prevention / Detection / Response / Recovery. By threat: Intrusion / Fraud / Abuse / Data-leak / Supply-chain / Insider. By response: Block / Step-up / Quarantine / Incident.
SEC.dataModel:
```yaml
SecurityEvent:
  securityEventId: <Identity>
  detectedBy: <registry detector id>
  severity: <registry level>
  subject: <Identity|null>
  context: <Context>
  evidence: [<Evidence>]
  response: <registry action>
  temporal: {detectedAt, respondedAt}
```
SEC.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Detected
    Detected --> Triaged
    Triaged --> Responded
    Responded --> Contained
    Contained --> Eradicated
    Eradicated --> Recovered
    Recovered --> [*]
    Triaged --> FalsePositive
```
workflow: detect → triage severity → respond automatically within bounds → escalate beyond bounds → incident → recover with evidence
authorities: Security Authority (response within bounds); incidents escalate to governance authority.
SEC.privacy: Security monitoring over personal behavior is minimized and consent-scoped; detection targets patterns, never contents.
SEC.audit: Every detection and response is evidence-backed; false positives are recorded, not deleted — they tune detectors.
SEC.twin: Security twin monitors detection coverage and response latency as the immune system's health.
SEC.agent: Security agents are the primary detectors — operating continuously within strict response bounds.
SEC.runtime: Guards are in-line and mandatory; response automation is bounded — escalation is always available to humans.
SEC.scaling: Detection is a stream job; response is synchronous for blocking severity, queued otherwise.
SEC.multiTenant: Security events are tenant-scoped; platform-level incidents aggregate anonymized signals only.
SEC.geo: Incident response routes to on-call in the affected jurisdiction — accountability is local.
SEC.failure: Detector blind spot, response latency, escalation queue overflow, quarantine exhaustion.
SEC.recovery: Recovery is a governed phase with evidence preservation — incidents end with post-mortems, not silent clears.
SEC.certification: Every request path must carry an enforcement record — an unguarded path is a critical certification failure.
SEC.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Detector
    participant SR as Security Runtime
    participant A as Authority
    D->>SR: signal
    SR->>SR: triage severity
    alt within bounds
        SR->>SR: auto-respond
    else beyond bounds
        SR->>A: escalate
        A-->>SR: decision
    end
    SR-->>D: outcome + evidence
```
SEC.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Detecting
    Detecting --> Triaging
    Triaging --> Responding
    Responding --> Recovering
```

DSP.concepts: Data Sovereignty Architecture ensures data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it belongs. Residency is a property of the data, enforced at storage, processing, replication, and egress — not a policy document.
DSP.ontology: Sovereignty binds a data class to a Jurisdiction context with a Residency policy, a Transfer policy, and an Egress policy. Data without a jurisdiction may not be written at all.
DSP.taxonomy: By control: Residency / Localization / Transfer-restricted / Sovereign-key. By scope: National / Regional / Sectoral / Contractual. By enforcement: Storage / Compute / Replication / Egress.
DSP.dataModel:
```yaml
SovereigntyBinding:
  bindingId: <Identity>
  dataClass: <registry id>
  jurisdiction: <Context>
  residencyPolicy: <Policy>
  transferPolicy: <Policy>
  egressPolicy: <Policy>
  temporal: {effectiveFrom}
```
DSP.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Bound
    Bound --> TransferRequested
    TransferRequested --> TransferAllowed: policy permits
    TransferRequested --> TransferDenied
    TransferAllowed --> Transferred
    Transferred --> [*]
```
workflow: classify data → bind jurisdiction → check residency at write → check transfer at replication → block egress at boundary
authorities: Jurisdiction Authority (binding); sovereignty overrides availability — a denied transfer is final, not retried.
DSP.privacy: Sovereignty is privacy's enforcement arm — residency makes legal rights practically enforceable.
DSP.audit: Every transfer attempt — allowed and denied — is logged with class, jurisdictions, and policy version.
DSP.twin: Sovereignty twin monitors replica placement continuously — drift triggers correction or alert.
DSP.agent: Sovereignty agent detects placement drift and flags unclassified data before it crosses a border.
DSP.runtime: Checks are in-line at write, replicate, and egress — sovereignty is a runtime gate, not a compliance report.
DSP.scaling: Binding lookup is cached per data class; egress inspection is at the boundary, not per-packet deep.
DSP.multiTenant: Tenants bind their own jurisdictions; shared infra respects every tenant's binding simultaneously — the strictest wins.
DSP.geo: This IS the geo architecture — jurisdiction bindings are the mechanism for all cross-region behavior.
DSP.failure: Unclassified data, binding conflict, replica drift, egress bypass attempt.
DSP.recovery: Placement violations trigger governed migration back into jurisdiction with full audit.
DSP.certification: Every data class must carry a binding — unbound data is uncertifiable and cannot be written.
DSP.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant SO as Sovereignty
    participant ST as Storage
    C->>SO: write(data, class)
    SO->>SO: resolve binding
    SO->>ST: route to jurisdiction
    ST-->>SO: stored in-region
    SO-->>C: ack
```
DSP.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Classifying
    Classifying --> Binding
    Binding --> ResidencyCheck
    ResidencyCheck --> Stored
```

CNS.concepts: Consent Architecture makes personal-data use a governed, revocable, auditable grant — not a clause. Consent is a first-class object with scope, purpose, duration, and a one-action revocation path.
CNS.ontology: Consent has a Subject (person), a Scope (data classes), a Purpose, a Grantee, a Duration, and a State. Consent scopes chain: withdrawn consent invalidates everything downstream, immediately and automatically.
CNS.taxonomy: By basis: Opt-in / Contract / Legal-obligation / Vital-interest / Legitimate-interest-governed. By scope: Broad / Purpose-specific / Narrow. By state: Given / Suspended / Withdrawn / Expired.
CNS.dataModel:
```yaml
Consent:
  consentId: <Identity>
  subject: <Identity>
  scope: [<registry data class>]
  purpose: <registry id>
  grantee: <Identity>
  basis: <registry id>
  temporal: {givenAt, expiresAt}
  state: <Given|Suspended|Withdrawn|Expired>
  lineage: {derivedFrom: <Consent|null>}
```
CNS.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested
    Requested --> Given: subject agrees
    Given --> Suspended
    Suspended --> Given
    Given --> Withdrawn
    Suspended --> Withdrawn
    Given --> Expired
    Withdrawn --> [*]
    Expired --> [*]
```
workflow: request with purpose + scope → subject grants → propagate to all consumers → withdrawal cascades immediately → verify before every use
authorities: Subject's own authority is supreme over their consent — no platform authority overrides withdrawal.
CNS.privacy: Consent IS the privacy control — purpose limitation is enforced at check time, not in policy prose.
CNS.audit: Every grant and withdrawal is logged with scope, purpose, and basis. Use-without-consent is a logged violation, not an error.
CNS.twin: Consent twin monitors expiry waves and withdrawal-propagation latency as privacy-health signals.
CNS.agent: Consent agent detects scope creep (use beyond granted purpose) and flags it for governance.
CNS.runtime: Checks are in-line before personal-data use; withdrawal invalidates caches and projections downstream.
CNS.scaling: Check is the hot path — cached per (subject, grantee, purpose) with event-driven invalidation on withdrawal.
CNS.multiTenant: Consent is subject-scoped, binding on all tenants holding the subject's data.
CNS.geo: Consent follows the subject's jurisdiction — withdrawal propagates globally regardless of data location.
CNS.failure: Withdrawal propagation gap, scope ambiguity, expiry storm, missing basis.
CNS.recovery: Withdrawal is immediate and complete — any delayed propagation is treated as a violation with remediation.
CNS.certification: Every personal-data use must cite a valid consent or legal basis — uncited use fails certification.
CNS.migration: New purposes and bases are registry additions.
CNS.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Subject
    participant CN as Consent
    participant U as Data Consumer
    S->>CN: withdraw(consent)
    CN->>CN: mark withdrawn
    CN->>U: propagate invalidation
    U->>U: purge + invalidate caches
    U-->>CN: confirmed
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requesting
    Requesting --> Granting
    Granting --> Propagating
    Propagating --> Enforced
```

SRE.concepts: Reliability Architecture treats uptime as a governed property: every capability declares an SLO, every breach burns a budget, and every recovery is rehearsed. Reliability is designed, not hoped for.
SRE.ontology: Reliability has SLOs (targets), Error budgets (governed spend), Dependencies (relationships), Failure domains (bounded blast radius), and Recovery objectives (RTO/RPO per class).
SRE.taxonomy: By criticality: Tier-0 (constitutional) / Tier-1 (critical) / Tier-2 (standard) / Tier-3 (best-effort). By metric: Availability / Latency / Durability / Correctness / Throughput. By recovery: RTO-immediate / RTO-hours / RTO-days.
SRE.dataModel:
```yaml
ReliabilityTarget:
  targetId: <Identity>
  capability: <registry capability>
  tier: <registry level>
  slo: {indicator, target, window}
  errorBudget: {remaining, resetsAt}
  dependencies: [<Relationship>]
  recovery: {rto, rpo}
  policy: <Policy>
```
SRE.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Healthy
    Healthy --> Degraded: SLO strain
    Degraded --> Breached: SLO breached
    Breached --> Frozen: budget exhausted
    Frozen --> Healthy: recovery + budget reset
    Degraded --> Healthy
```
workflow: declare SLO → measure continuously → burn budget on errors → freeze on exhaustion → recover → rehearse
authorities: Reliability Authority (SLO governance); freeze halts non-critical change under policy.
SRE.privacy: Reliability metrics carry no personal data by construction — indicators are aggregate.
SRE.audit: Every breach and freeze is logged with cause analysis and remediation; rehearsals are recorded.
SRE.twin: Reliability twin simulates failure scenarios against live topology — chaos engineering under governance.
SRE.agent: Reliability agent detects budget burn early and proposes freezes before exhaustion.
SRE.runtime: Probes are continuous; circuit breakers are automatic; fallbacks degrade gracefully, never silently.
SRE.scaling: Failure domains are bounded per tier; blast radius is a queryable property, not a guess.
